newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: Anger turns to tears as Port Arthur gunman confesses.
newsitem.headline: Anger turns to tears as Port Arthur gunman confesses.

text.p: Anger dissolved into tears on Thursday after Martin Bryant admitted to slaying 35 people at Port Arthur in a confession expected to release a wave of pent-up grief in Tasmania's close-knit island community.

Despite laughing and smirking throughout Thursday morning's brief court appearance, Bryant's unexplained decision to reverse his earlier pleas of innocence brought instant tears to the eyes of traumatised relatives and survivors of the April massacre.

In contrast to Bryant's previous court appearance six weeks ago -- when his not-guilty pleas were met with a cry of "You're a bloody coward!" from a man whose brother died in the massacre -- Thursday's bizarre court proceedings were tinged with relief.

The 16 or so bereaved family and witnesses who attended the Supreme Court of Tasmania hearing were later shepherded out of the small, windowless courtroom without making any comment to the news media, which were warned to respect their privacy.
On April 28, Bryant opened fire with a high-powered rifle shooting dead 35 people at the historic Port Arthur convict site on Tasmania's southeast coast.
The Port Arthur Recovery Centre, which was set up during the massacre to treat hundreds of people for shock and trauma, said Bryant's confession was a relief from emotional suffering.
"It's sort of an end to a chapter and a closure for them. They can put it behind them and go on with their lives," the centre's co-ordinator, Rod MacGregor, told Reuters.

"People have, I think, kept their grief in check to an extent in expectation of the trial coming along, and (now) they may well move onto the next phase of some quite intense grieving," MacGregor said.

Tasmania's island community has been deeply shaken by the events of April 28, when Bryant took a semi-automatic rifle out of a tennis bag and opened fire on tourists enjoying a fine autumn day among the ruins of Port Arthur's old penal colony.
Bryant opened fire in Port Arthur's crowded Broad Arrow Cafe as vistors ate their lunch, claiming the first 20 lives within minutes. Witnesses later likened the scene to a battle field.
"Those memories will be there forever," survivor Peter Crosswell told reporters after the massacre, choking back tears.
Memorial services held soon after the shootings unleashed an outpouring of grief and soothing words around the country, but dozens of people remained in their own private hell.
"In most instances like this, there are 10 to 15 percent of people who experience quite severe post-traumatic stress disorders," MacGregor said.
"They need extensive work. They'll have serious problems with eating or with sleeplessness. They might not be able to leave their homes because of anxiety, fears and panic attacks."
The massacre also touched many Tasmanians who escaped the line of fire, MacGregor said.

"People are still coming forward...A lot of people would not appreciate why they might be having fights with their spouse or their partner and that it might be something to do with the general shock in the community," he said.
Tasmania state's chief prosector, Damian Bugg, and Bryant's own lawyer joined others on Thursday in expressing reflief that witnesses had been spared the additional anguish of a trial.
"I am relieved for their sake and for the community's sake," Bugg told reporters outside the court.
